articles.title: I can’t get enough of the iPhone Duo’s matte inner display
articles.summary: Apple’s iPhone Duo features a nano-texture finish on its inner screen, making it easier on the eyes.
articles.body: The iPhone Duo has all the messiness of a first-gen product. And while I’m not sure I love all of the decisions Apple made around its design, it got one thing right: the matte finish on the inner screen. I’ve been using it for the past week to watch movies on a plane, peruse my photo gallery, and catch up on a little reading, and I’m convinced. The matte screen is the best thing about the Duo, and I hope every other foldable maker copies it. When we first got our hands on the Duo, the nano-texture finish on the 7.6-inch inner screen was genuinely a surprise. I’ve used a dozen or so book-style foldables over the past five years, and every one of them came with a glossy inner display. Aside from occasionally noting that they can be hard to see in direct sun, I never really questioned it. That’s just how screens are, I figured. But opening up the Duo for the first time, it clicked. Matte makes sense. [Image: If you want to watch a podcast video outside, the matte screen has you covered. The benefits proved out while I used the phone for the past seven days. I propped it up on my tray table to watch an episode of Widow’s Bay. The matte screen effectively fought off the glare from the open window in my row. Reading a longer article felt a little easier on the eyes, and that’s what the inner screen is really there for. And there’s something about that slight matte finish that signals to my brain that it’s time to read. I can sort of fool myself into thinking that I’m holding an e-reader when I open the Kindle app and turn the phone sideways to its portrait orientation. It’s cute to imagine using your reading app in the landscape-oriented, partway-closed posture like a physical book. But I wouldn’t actually read anything like that; portrait all the way. The thing to know about the Duo’s matte finish is that it’s pretty subtle. You don’t feel it under your finger quite as much as the more paperlike finish on TCL’s Nxtpaper devices. My colleague Dominic Preston wondered if it would be jarring flipping between the glossy cover screen and the matte display, and personally it hasn’t bothered me. The fact that the Duo’s big screen isn’t full-on e-reader matte probably helps ease that transition. [Image: Maybe blacks don’t look as rich as they could on a glossy display, but I’m okay with that. In fact, changing between the two screens somehow feels nice in both directions. Opening up to the inner screen feels like a welcome break from the reflections on the outer screen. When closing it and going back to the outer screen, the richer blacks and colors feel inviting. I can concede that if you’re watching something with a lot of dark, shadowy scenes, the matte might feel like it obscures a bit of the detail that would otherwise stand out. It didn’t really bother me. But the bottom line is that this is a device that you will, by its nature, take outside. You’ll use it in ideal lighting conditions and crappy ones. I’ll take a slight hit in richness and detail for a more comfortable overall viewing experience. When my seatmate throws the window shade open, I’ll be ready for it.

articles.title: The iPhone Duo is a messy, expensive, good time
articles.summary: Apple’s first foldable is an early adopter special.
articles.body: The iPhone Duo is the riskiest Apple product in years. It’s a huge rethink of what an iPhone is and could be, and it contains the seeds of many fascinating ideas that might be great in the future. But that future is yet to come. The iPhone Duo is also one of Apple’s messiest first-generation products in a long time, and right now it will delight gadget nerds and early adopters and likely frustrate everyone else. It’s been a minute since the iPhone has looked or worked significantly differently. The last major change was the iPhone X, which dropped the home button almost a decade ago, and even that was a fairly subtle improvement. In fact, “subtle improvement” is really the entire story of the iPhone — it’s the foundation of Apple’s entire business, after all, and there’s a lot of risk in just up and changing it. You can see it in this year’s iPhone 18 Pro: It’s been refined in many ways, with better thermals and an interesting variable aperture lens, but it’s barely different than the iPhone 17 Pro. But you can’t play it safe designing a foldable. You have to make some big decisions about screen sizes and what the inner and outer displays are for, and then make an even bigger set of decisions about how that big inner screen should work. All of those decisions are risky, and Apple’s riskiest decision was the Duo’s size and shape. [Product: iPhone Duo | Hardware and design Apple’s single most important design decision for the Duo was to make it shaped like a passport. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: The wide aspect ratio makes the inner screen friendlier for 16:9 YouTube videos, but it also marks a departure from the taller foldable design phone makers have embraced over the past five years. Prior to 2026, most folding phones opted for a tall-and-narrow shape to optimize for using vertical apps on the cover screen. But rumors started pointing to Apple going with its landscape-first form factor, and other foldable makers shifted gears — seemingly to get ahead of Apple. Now that the iPhone and a handful of competitors have adopted the wide format, they have to solve a new problem: designing a cover screen that will work well enough for vertically oriented apps. The Duo’s 5.4-inch outer display is glossy, while the 7.6-inch inner display has a striking nano-texture matte coating. Apple’s very proud of this inner matte display, and for good reason — it looks and feels incredibly solid, a big step up from foldables with glossy, seemingly soft screens with glaringly obvious creases, like the Pixel Fold, and even the more subtle but still visible crease of the Galaxy Fold 8. [Image: [Image: [Image: The matte display is indeed there to help hide the crease, which Apple keeps calling “perceptually flat” because it’s more fun to invent science-y marketing phrases than just saying “you mostly don’t see it.” But it’s true: You mostly can’t see the display crease, although you can definitely feel it. If you’re looking at a white image off-axis, you can see it, and there are moments in some lighting where it’s much more obvious. It definitely shows up more prominently on camera than it does to your eyes. [Image: What you will see is the under-display camera, which reflects light in a more glossy way if you’re outdoors or in a bright area. Overall, though, the camera and display crease stopped being noticeable after a while. The crease also wasn’t any more noticeable after a week of constant flipping and folding, although we’ll see how it holds up over time. That’ll be a real test, because Duo owners are going to be constantly flipping this thing open. Between Apple’s display aspect ratio and iOS design choices, the outer screen feels like much more of a status display than you’d expect — everything about the Duo gently nudges you to flip it open and use it in tablet mode. And not just tablet mode, but portrait tablet mode. That’s because iPhone apps are largely portrait, and the Duo is still very much an iPhone, even though its shape makes it fight all that history. iPhones have gotten bigger over the years, but they’ve mostly stuck to the same basic rectangular aspect ratios: 2:3 from the first iPhone through the 4S, 16:9 from the iPhone 5 through the 8, and 19.5:9 from the iPhone X on to today’s iPhone 18 Pro. Basically, the iPhone has mostly gotten taller over time. The Duo changes all of that — it’s the first iPhone that’s gotten shorter and wider. Both the inner and outer displays have a 1.4:1 aspect ratio, which was a very deliberate choice on Apple’s part, because they’re the same shape open and closed. This is clever in terms of display math and potentially great for app developers, but in practice it means that the outer display is really quite small, especially compared to modern Max-sized phones. If you’re texting someone in Messages with the keyboard onscreen, you’re lucky to be able to see two or three texts at once. Apple has tried to reclaim some vertical space by scooting the UI elements of updated apps off to the right, but if you’re left-handed, that means using the phone closed with one hand can be challenging, even for someone with big hands. Having that strip of real estate along the right side occupied by navigation controls also means that using the Duo single-handed in your right forces you to reach farther when there’s something on the left side of the screen you need to tap. This means that you’re sometimes holding a fairly heavy phone, stretching for a small target that’s just out of reach, which isn’t particularly confidence-inspiring. It’s also wild to have iPhone apps with controls in all kinds of different places; reaching for the back button in Apple’s Mail app and realizing it’s moved from the top left to the right is kind of disorienting. A lot of using the Duo is just figuring out how to use an iPhone again, which hasn’t happened in a long time. [Image: If you’re using an app that isn’t updated for the Duo, you’ll see a black bar along the right side of the cover screen where those navigation controls would otherwise live. But even updated apps don’t feel particularly useful for anything other than a quick check-in on the cover screen. Apple says you’re getting 90 percent of the screen area of an iPhone 18 Pro, but that’s pretty small for today’s apps. It’s like having an iPhone 5 in a world of iPhone Pro Maxes. This means that when you pull the Duo out of your pocket, you’ll almost always be looking at a tiny amount of information. And the second you want to really do anything, you’ll find yourself unfolding the phone to use the vastly larger and more useful inner display. But you don’t get any additional height when you open the Duo up. Switching from a tiny portrait display to a bigger landscape view isn’t useful for most phone apps, which are all designed around big portrait displays. Most phone apps look silly this way, especially those still running as standard iPhone apps, which look normal but with lots of black padding on either side. It’s either cramped and tiny on the outer screen or a little silly and awkward when you open the Duo. This means almost every time you open the phone you instinctively rotate it, and while it will work no matter how it’s rotated, it’s better to rotate it counterclockwise so the cameras are on top and the volume buttons are on the top left. Over our week of testing, this started feeling more natural, but it’s exactly the opposite of what you’d initially expect. It’s especially odd in Apple’s bumper case, which has a large notch to expose the Touch ID sensor and camera control, and it looks for all the world like it belongs at the bottom. [Image: You might think this is a little thing, but it’s strange to find yourself slightly unsure of how to hold a smartphone. A nontrivial part of the Duo experience is just reorienting yourself to where the volume buttons are as you flip the thing around. When closed, they’re on top of the phone, but if you rotate the Duo clockwise, they end up on the bottom right, and it’s the top button that turns the volume down because they don’t change orientation with the display. There’s a buried setting in iOS that makes the volume buttons reorient themselves as you turn the Duo around; Apple needs to set it so it works right by default. One other thing to get used to is simply unlocking the phone. Touch ID is integrated into the wake button on the side of the phone. There’s no Face ID at all, and it might take a minute to remember that when you stare at your phone for a beat and wonder why your notifications aren’t unfurling. Ask us how we know. But a week is long enough to get used to Touch ID life again, and it’s mostly painless once you remember you’re supposed to be using it. [Image: Now, here’s the thing: This is all pretty fun! The iPhone has been the same for so long that being forced to come up with little moves and tricks and ways to think about holding the Duo is a gadget nerd thrill. Other foldables do this too — Samsung and Google and Huawei have been pushing the envelope of gadget-y smartphones for ages — but Apple’s played it so safe for so long that the Duo is legitimately surprising. But Apple hasn’t found some magical software solution to making a product with this much inherent complexity any less chaotic. It just happens to be the kind of first-generation chaos that will delight early adopters and lead most everyone else back to their regular old iPhones. Software [Image: That first-generation wonkiness is most obvious in the software, especially in how the Duo supports third-party apps. Almost everyone who sees the Duo assumes that it simply opens up into being an iPad, but that’s not how it works at all. In classic Apple fashion, the company decided to throw everything out and start over. That means getting rid of a lot of weird iPad baggage, but it also means that solved problems on the iPad are back on the Duo. It’s big stuff and little stuff: For whatever reason, the Duo doesn’t support pinching the keyboard to make it smaller and friendlier to use one-handed — a feature iPads have had for ages. It also means there are new ways to think about multitasking, and sometimes you’ll be unsure what will happen when you swipe around the screen because apps interact with iOS and each other in very different ways. [Image: If you want to run two apps at once on the Duo, you swipe up and over to pin an app to one side, and then pin another app to the other side. If you tap on the little divider, you connect the apps into a set, and you can come right back to it in the app switcher. It’s neat, but it only works in landscape. If you want to have two apps open when you’re holding the Duo in portrait mode, you’re basically out of luck — unless what you want is to watch a video on the top while scrolling an app on the bottom. In that case, you need to make sure you have an app that supports background video, open that app, start the video, close that app to initiate the floating video window, open your other app, and then (and only then!) find a little button in the floating video window and hit that to pop everything into place. This is legitimately cool once you figure it out. But you will note that this is a totally different approach to multitasking than any previous iPhone or iPad, and nothing about the Duo’s interface makes it obvious that it can work this way. It’s a lot of these little moments of figuring it out for yourself that really solidify the Duo as an early adopter special — especially since some features only work in some apps sometimes. That floating video feature? Yeah, it works with YouTube TV, but it doesn’t seem to work with regular YouTube. This is initially surprising, because the YouTube app appears to be at least a little updated for the Duo. But it turns out that right now there are basically three ways apps work on the Duo. --- iPhone Duo AMA Got more questions about the Duo? Verge subscribers can post their questions over to our AMA where senior reviewer Allison Johnson will be answering them starting at 11:30AM ET. --- First, there are regular iPhone apps that haven’t been updated at all. As with an iPad, you can zoom and rotate these apps to make things a little more useful, but they look pretty silly. This is the vast majority of apps right now, although we saw lots of apps get updated to the second category during the course of our review. The second category is what you might call the messy middle: apps that have been updated for iOS 27. They get some automatic layout fixes so they’ll automatically expand to fill the inner screen in landscape orientation and don’t look quite as silly as standard iPhone apps. But you can tell they haven’t actually been designed for these displays, and those rough edges are super obvious. The telltale sign of these apps is the black bar on the right when you use them on the cover screen — proper Duo apps add controls to that space, but these in-between apps don’t. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: Then there are fully updated Duo apps built for the Duo-specific iOS 27.1 — we got to test a few of these, and they can be pretty good. Instagram’s Edits app is a perfect example of why a folding phone is useful. It opens into a full video editor with a big timeline and nice preview window, and you can just get things done. And even in the span of the past week that we’ve been using the Duo, we’ve seen some apps, like Slack, go from the messy middle to fully updated. This makes a big difference in how useful they feel on the inner screen, but obviously doesn’t address the reality of the small outer-screen real estate. Developers will need to have either a lot of energy to create neat stuff that takes advantage of the Duo’s form factor or a lot of encouragement from Apple. Maybe both. Either way, we have to hand it to the Deck-Man app, which reformats Apple Music into a little virtual Walkman. The page-turn animation in Books is terrific. And if you’ve ever dreamed of reading PDFs on a big screen in the back of an Uber, know that they look particularly great on the matte display. But the reality is you’re going to see a lot of tiny iPhone apps and apps in the weird unoptimized middle zone for a while. It’s all just messy, in a lot of the same ways Android foldables are. That’s particularly surprising because the Android tablet app story has always been messy, but Apple had the whole ecosystem of iPad apps waiting at the ready. For whatever reason, the company just didn’t go that way, and that means it will take a while for the Duo’s app story to settle down. Versus the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 The Duo’s most obvious competitor is the Galaxy Z Fold 8, which Samsung managed to sneak out a few months ahead of the Duo. They’re both wide folds, but they’re not exactly the same. The Fold 8’s front screen is slightly taller and narrower, and the Duo is noticeably thicker and heavier. Those details add up to a big difference in how it feels to use the cover screen, especially one-handed. The Duo is pretty hard to use single-handed, but it feels doable with the Fold 8. [Image: Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8. Apple also insists on preserving the more narrow vertical aspect ratio when you use an app on the cover screen by reserving that strip on the side for controls, whereas Samsung lets content occupy the entire width of the screen. On the larger inner display, Samsung offers a couple of options to make the keyboard friendlier to use. You can switch to a one-handed option that’s easier to reach or a floating keyboard you can move around and resize. And lots more Android apps readily take advantage of the full inner screen because foldables have been a thing on Android for quite a while now. [Image: Apple is really emphasizing the ability to use the Duo in a variety of postures, including that kind of “I’m reading a book” situation where it’s partially closed. You can prop the phone up in tent mode and use it as a clock or digital photo frame. If you use it as an alarm, you’ll get a nice glow from the inner screen that’s supposed to help gently wake you up. You can watch videos on half of the inner screen in laptop mode, or on the outer screen in tent mode. Weirdly, Apple is actually more liberal in this than Samsung. The half-open position is called Flex mode on other Galaxy foldables, but the Z Fold 8 doesn’t let you use it, probably because the hinge isn’t stiff enough all the way through its range of motion. [Image: Another important difference: The Duo is rated IP68 for full water and dust resistance, while the Z Fold 8 is IP48, so it isn’t fully dust-resistant. Neither phone should be used carelessly at the beach, but that higher dust rating offers a little more peace of mind. Overall, these feel like pretty familiar moves for both of these companies. Apple wants you to use its phone its way. Samsung is less hung up on details like aspect ratios and where the keyboard can be. As always, Apple’s phone works best the deeper you are in the walled garden. The Duo feels a little more polished, but the Z Fold 8 has the better cover screen experience. Given how much of the experience of a foldable is reliant on the cover screen, that counts for a lot. Performance and battery life [Image: We each tested our own review units under pretty different circumstances over the past week, so it’s not surprising our battery life experiences differed. Nilay used the Duo just like he would during any other workday, using Slack, Google Docs, and Safari, and watching YouTube TV, Instagram, and TikTok. He needed to charge the Duo at least once to get through the day. This matched his usual experience with regular Pro iPhones, although the MagSafe battery packs he uses to get through the day are made for taller iPhones and don’t fit the Duo very well. Allison was traveling more with the Duo, and spent more time watching video on Wi-Fi on her flights and scrolling social media. She had about 30 percent left after about 6.5 hours of screen-on time, which is decent. But as ever, iPhone battery life tends to vary dramatically for everyone, and change a lot over time. That’s even more so the case with a foldable — the more you use the inner screen, the worse of a time you’ll have with the battery. Performance-wise, the Duo has an A20 Pro chip, and Apple says it has the same improved vapor chamber thermal management system as the iPhone 18 Pro. For most things it’s plenty fast, but the reality is that it’s also a thin phone driving two big displays, and it definitely gets warm, and sometimes hot. We saw this happen in two places: third-party apps, particularly video apps and Google’s apps, caused things to get hot. The first-generation nature of the Duo really came through here, and it’s something we would hope would improve as various apps get updated. The phone also heats up when you use the camera for a long time — especially features that use the camera and both displays at once, like Duo Preview and Kid Cue. You can just feel the phone getting significantly hotter when this happens. Add in processor-intensive camera features like Smart Take, which automatically hits the shutter button, and the phone gets hot enough to start noticeably lagging after a while. You’d hope Apple can improve battery life and thermal management over time — it has certainly done that with other iPhones in the past. But the Duo today gets hot, and doesn’t seem ready to last a full day of heavy use. Those are real compromises on a phone that starts at $2,000. Camera [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: The Duo’s other big compromise is camera quality. It has a smaller main camera sensor than the one you’ll find in the 18 Pro and is instead on par with what you get from the iPhone Air. That’s fine for grabbing everyday shots, but it’s fundamentally a notch below flagship tier. The Duo relies on heavier sharpening to make up for its weaker hardware, so fine details look a little crunchier than they do on the 18 Pro. The Duo retains a bit less color detail in low light too, though Night Mode kind of evens out the playing field between them. [Image: [Image: Some of the manual controls on the 18 Pro are absent here, too. There’s no shutter speed and no moving aperture, but you do get white balance and manual focus controls. The biggest concession is that there’s no telephoto camera here. You get that 2x crop zoom and up to just 10x digital zoom. There’s a 48-megapixel ultrawide that’s fine, but you just don’t have the flexibility you’ll find on basically every slab phone that costs half as much as the Duo. The 12-megapixel Center Stage selfie camera on the front screen is a little worse than the 18-megapixel one on the 18 Pro — again, it looks like it’s compensating for its lower resolution by oversharpening details. There’s also an under-display FaceTime camera on the inner screen that’s okay in good light but really quite bad in dim light. (Apple won’t say the FaceTime camera’s resolution, but it’s just 4 megapixels.) Overall, it’s serviceable for a video call, but not much else. [Image: [Image: [Image: But the good thing about a folding phone is that every camera on this thing is a selfie camera. You can open it up and preview your image on the front display while you use the much better main camera to take a photo of yourself. You’ll actually want to use the camera control button on purpose for a change, because it’s the only sensible way to press the shutter when you have the phone facing you like this — there’s no on-screen shutter and the volume controls are right next to the lens. Apple’s Kid Cue takes a page out of Google’s book by using the front screen to play animations designed to get your kid looking at the camera. It works, but your subject will be looking off to the side since the Duo (wisely) uses the better main camera lens rather than the selfie camera for this. But if you’ve ever tried to get a young kid to look at a camera and make a normal face, you’ll probably agree that this is close enough. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: Outside of that, the form factor lets you do a couple of fun things with the camera. You can set it up in laptop mode or standing up like a book to shoot a time-lapse. There’s a feature called Smart Take that will automatically snap photos when it senses that subjects in the frame are striking a pose that’s kinda fun. (It would be cool if you could switch the image preview to the other panel to use it halfway open like a waist-level viewfinder, but you can’t.) [Image: The main camera records up to 4K/120 video and it will let you apply Cinematic mode to your clips after capture like the 18 Pro does. You also get the new texture controls in Photographic Styles if you want your foldable phone camera to act more like a film camera. Still, you’re definitely not getting the latest and greatest iPhone camera, which is weird on a $2,000 phone — though that’s certainly not unusual for a foldable. On the other side of the aisle, Samsung basically split its Fold series into two models: the wide one with less-good cameras and the portrait-oriented one with a better main camera. You can’t have everything — unless you have access to foldables sold in China, in which case, yeah you can. The bottom line is that the Duo offers a totally acceptable camera for a new iPhone, but it’s far from the best iPhone camera you can get. Bits and bobs [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: There’s a lot of other little stuff to say about the Duo — it’s full of new ideas and weird little details keep coming up the more you use it. The Duo has MagSafe, unlike the Z Fold 8, which is a big quality-of-life improvement. Allison found that a PopSocket made the Duo way easier to hold, while Nilay had a less-good time trying to use his existing MagSafe battery packs on the phone. He also has MagSafe mounts around his house and stuck the phone up all over the place, with entertaining results. Who hasn’t dreamed of having a tablet in the shower? You can use the Duo like a tiny little laptop, which is adorable, and it connects to a portable keyboard for some purse computer action. You can also watch movies and TV shows with it slightly bent, so it stays open on a table in tent mode. (It takes a second for the phone to figure out that you want to do this, but it gets there.) If all of this sounds stressful, then the first-gen foldable life might not be for you. But if you’re itching to try some of this out for yourself, then you just might be the kind of early adopter who will have a good time with the Duo. The wrap-up [Image: The hard rule at The Verge for 15 years now is that you have to review the product that’s in the box — not the idea of the product, or all of our hopes and dreams, or even the promise of software updates to come. (And boy, does the Duo have a lot of software and app updates to come.) There’s a lot of potential in the Duo, but right now it is a first-gen device in every possible way. It is expensive, it’s full of compromises, and it can be incredibly frustrating to use. Switching from the Duo back to one of our standard slab phones to get something done often felt like a relief. Sometimes you just need your iPhone to do what you need it to do — that’s why Apple has been so risk-averse in changing it. But all of the risk and weirdness of the Duo is also fun, in the way the best early adopter devices are fun. It’s incomplete as a product, but complete enough as an idea that you can see where things are going. It’s reminiscent of the very first MacBook Air, which took exactly no one by storm — it took a full redesign for Apple to get it right, and then it took over the entire industry. We’ll see what happens with the Duo, but as it stands, it is very much an open question whether Apple made the right choices about the Duo’s screen sizes and aspect ratios. Most Duo owners will find that the cover display is simply too small to use all the time. Avoiding the entire iPad app ecosystem is another choice that might not age well; so is asking developers to jump on board with a device that’s clearly destined to eventually run into the iPad. Apple also made some very real compromises around the camera, and we’ll need to do a lot more testing to understand the Duo’s performance and thermal management story. But the Duo is a more cohesive idea about foldables than most of its Android competition, precisely because Apple has a better app and developer story to lean on. Right now the problem for most Android foldables is that the inner screens aren’t that useful so there’s no super compelling reason to open them. The problem with the Duo is that the outer screen isn’t useful enough, so you want to open it all the time, and Apple’s ecosystem means that eventually the apps will be useful on the inner screen. But the real answer is somewhere in the middle — for both screens to be interesting and useful. Someone’s going to get there, and we’ll see if Apple can be the first.

articles.title: I reviewed the iPhone Duo, ask me anything
articles.summary: Our review of the iPhone Duo is live, and we know you have more questions. Subscribers can get them answered now.
articles.body: I’m The Verge’s senior smartphone reviewer and I’ve been using the iPhone Duo for the past week. I’ve unfolded it, flipped it, and folded it more times than I could count as I’ve been working on the review alongside our editor-in-chief Nilay Patel, and I’m ready to answer your questions about it. The Duo represents the first time the iPhone has gone through a major form factor shift, and in true Apple fashion, it has some very specific ideas about how you should use it. We covered a lot of how the Duo works in our review, but there’s a ton more to talk about and I am here for it. Verge subscribers can submit questions starting right now in the comments and I’ll start answering later today at 8:30AM PT / 11:30AM ET.

articles.title: Blink brings 4K to its low-cost security camera lineup
articles.summary: Amazon is launching a new lineup of Blink security cameras, including its first 4K, spotlight, and pan-tilt models.
articles.body: Amazon is launching a new lineup of Blink security cameras, including its first 4K, pan-tilt models, and battery-powered spotlight models. These new additions provide better resolution and extended range for monitoring your property compared to Blink’s current Mini 2K, Mini 2K Plus, and Outdoor 2K Plus offerings, with a variety of different specializations to best suit your security requirements. One of the standouts is the $199.99 Blink Frontier XR Plus, a trail camera that’s designed for expansive properties that would typically require multiple cameras or specialized monitoring equipment. It can cover up to 7,000 feet with a clear line of sight, making this Blink’s farthest-reaching camera to date. There’s also the $79.99 Blink Mini 4K Plus, Blink’s first camera to support 4K resolution. It’s suitable for indoor and outdoor use, and features Wi-Fi 6 support, two-way audio, and Smart Alerts with person and vehicle detection. The $109.99 Spotlight Cam 2K Plus and $49.99 Mini Pan-Tilt 2K Plus are also included in the launch, as Blink’s first battery-powered spotlight and pan-tilt cameras respectively. The Mini Pan-Tilt 2K Plus is the most affordable offering in the new lineup, providing 350-degrees of pan and 115-degrees of tilt alongside night vision, two-way audio, and motion detection for people and vehicles to track where the action is happening. The $149.99 Blink Outdoor 2K XR Plus rounds out the collection. It can reach up to 800 feet away with some obstructions, or up to 2,700 feet with a clear line of sight. Eligible features like video descriptions, motion-activated notifications, and 60 days of cloud video storage are available as an optional subscription that starts at $3.99 per month, or you can otherwise record locally on a Blink Sync Module. All five cameras are available for preorder starting today in the US, though availability in other regions will vary by model. Blink hasn’t specified when the cameras will start shipping, so we’ve asked for clarification and will update if we hear back.

articles.title: Apple says it only has ‘limited’ iPhone Duo units for in-store sales
articles.summary: Apple says it will have “limited” iPhone Duo models available in stores when the device launches on October 23rd, according to Reuters.
articles.body: Apple says it will have “limited” iPhone Duo models for sale in stores, according to a report from Reuters. The iPhone Duo launches on Friday, October 23rd, but online preorders quickly sold out, with some delivery estimates extending into next year. “On Friday morning, our teams look forward ​to welcoming customers at Apple Stores to experience iPhone Duo ​and the incredible iPhone line-up for themselves,” Apple said in a statement to Reuters. “Apple Stores will ‌have ⁠limited iPhone Duo available for walk-in customers, and we’re working hard to get this revolutionary new product into customers’ hands as quickly as possible.” The iPhone Duo will be available with “limited” walk-in availability in the US, Canada, Australia, Mexico, and most of the UK and Europe, according to Reuters. Customers in these countries will also be able to pick up their online orders in store. Meanwhile, customers in mainland China, France, Hong Kong, India, Japan, Malaysia, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand, and ⁠the ​United Arab Emirates will only be able to pick up their online iPhone Duo orders in stores. Apple didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment. The iPhone Duo is Apple’s first foldable, offering a 5.4-inch outer display and 7.6-inch inner screen. It starts at $1,999, and recent reports have suggested that the company might not have enough to make available in stores on a walk-in basis due to supply constraints. Update, October 21st: Added Apple’s statement to Reuters.

articles.title: Samsung’s 5K monitor has good gaming chops and a great price
articles.summary: The Samsung 27-inch G80HF gaming monitor is down to $599.99 and sports up to a 5K resolution at 180Hz, or 1440p at 360Hz. You can also save on a GTA 6 bundle.
articles.body: There are quite a few 5K monitors out there. Many of them are designed to appeal to Mac users who are looking for cheaper Studio Display alternatives without giving up the pixel-dense 218ppi screen. However, if you’re interested in hearing about one with gaming chops, Samsung’s 27-inch Odyssey G80HF seems like one of the best monitors out there to satisfy your niche, but respectable desires. Currently, you can grab this model for $599.99 at Amazon and B&H Photo, which beats its best price by $100. [Product: Samsung 27-inch Odyssey G8 5K monitor | The G80HF supports two display modes with its Fast IPS panel: 5K at up to 180Hz refresh rate, or 1440p with up to a 360Hz refresh rate. Samsung touts Nvidia G-Sync compatibility as well as AMD FreeSync Premium to ensure the monitor’s refresh rate remains in lockstep with your GPU’s frame rate output. The monitor features a DisplayPort 2.1 port (just one, and Samsung doesn’t advertise its bandwidth), two HDMI 2.1 ports, and a USB hub for charging or connecting two USB-A 3.2 Gen 1 accessories. As a gamer, one of my favorite features here is the one-millisecond response time. That’s a very common spec among gaming monitors — even in ones that cost hundreds less — but it’s a bit of a rare spec in a 5K monitor at this price. I tested KTC’s sub-$500 model last year, and gaming on it was a pretty atrocious experience despite having what it claimed to be gaming-ready capabilities. For $200 more ($799.99), LG’s 27-inch UltraGear evo 5K Mini LED monitor delivers slightly better specs. It has more dimming zones for a more accurate picture, it can get brighter, and it supports USB-C video input with 90W power delivery output to charge your device as you use it. Its dual mode refresh rates aren’t as high as Samsung’s (165Hz / 330Hz), but I don’t really see that as much of a downside. Other great deals happening now * For those who haven’t yet placed a preorder for Grand Theft Auto VI, which comes out in less than a month, you can do so while saving $10 on a gaming gift card at Best Buy. The retailer is letting customers build a bundle of select games and gift cards. You can, for example, add GTA VI and a gift card will be $10 off its advertised price at checkout. It’s a small, but welcome way to save a little cash. The bundle includes other current and upcoming blockbusters, like Gears of War: E-Day, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, and more. * The excellent remake of Demon’s Souls by the shuttered PlayStation studio, Bluepoint Games, is down to just $13.49 in digital format on the PlayStation Store. What’s more, it’s for the digital deluxe edition (originally $89.99), which includes in-game cosmetics, a consumable that grants you a bunch of souls for in-game upgrades, and the soundtrack. The sale lasts through November 4th on the West Coast, or until 2:59AM ET on November 5th on the East Coast. The remake doesn’t mess with the formula of FromSoftware’s PS3 cult classic (it has stages instead of being an open-world like its spiritual successor, Dark Souls), but gives it some brilliant visuals and fast loading times. It’s definitely worth a try if you’re into other Soulslike games that reward (and test) your patience. Read our review of the game. * If you need a multi-port wall charger to quickly charge a bunch of USB-C devices, Ugreen’s Nexode Pro is down to $59.99 at Amazon and Ugreen, a $30 discount off the usual cost. The price was $10 lower during June’s Prime Day, but this is still a nice value. Despite the charger advertising 160W charging passthrough, its USB-C ports labeled C1 and C2 each top out at 140W when just one device is plugged into the charger. The power of each port (four USB-C, one USB-A) varies depending on how many gadgets are plugged in, up to 160W total. The charger has folding prongs and a display that can rotate depending on how it’s plugged in.

articles.title: Samsung’s latest 55-inch Frame TV is down to its lowest price yet
articles.summary: Samsung’s latest 55-inch Frame TV is $400 off at Amazon. The art-inspired TV features a matte display, customizable bezels, and access to thousands of artworks.
articles.body: If you want a TV but prefer something that won’t clash with your room’s decor, Samsung’s The Frame is a standout option that’s designed to look like a piece of framed art instead of a black, monolithic rectangle mounted to your wall. You can buy the latest version of the 55-inch Samsung Frame TV on sale for around $897.99 ($402 off) at Amazon, which marks a new low price. Larger sizes are on sale, too, including the new 98-inch model, which is down to $3,749.99 ($1,252 off). [Product: Samsung The Frame TV (2026) | The 2026 model is largely the same as its predecessor; The biggest hardware change is that this size of the TV features built-in ports instead of using Samsung’s One Connect Box. Like previous models, it has a matte, canvas-like display that more closely resembles an actual painting better than a glossy TV screen. Its built-in motion sensor detects when someone enters the room and can automatically display artwork, even adjusting its brightness and colors based on ambient lighting. It supports Samsung’s Art Store, which offers access to more than 5,000 works ranging from world-famous galleries to lesser known, independent artists. A full subscription costs $49.99 annually, though you can also enjoy 30 new free, rotating artworks every month. Samsung includes a wall mount and a black bezel in the box, with additional magnetic frame styles available separately to better match your space or taste. In terms of performance, the Frame prioritizes style over image quality, so it’s not necessarily the best choice for cinephiles who may be willing to pay more for a brighter picture, deeper blacks, and more lifelike colors. Still it offers a refresh rate of up to 144Hz with variable refresh rate support for smoother gaming, along with HDR10 Plus and Dolby Atmos support for a more immersive audio/visual experience. articles.title: GM promises smarter cars, faster updates, and autonomous dry-cleaning runs
articles.summary: General Motors announced it will use AI to cut vehicle development times in half, improve EV battery range, and install compute units up to 40 times more powerful.
articles.body: General Motors is still very much in the business of selling gas-guzzling trucks and massive SUVs. But if you listen to its leadership, the Detroit giant is rapidly transforming into a nimble, software-defined tech player with a tightened grip on AI. That was the pitch today, when GM hosted its tech-focused Onward event to unveil a wide-ranging slate of EV, autonomous vehicle, and AI initiatives — all aimed at fending off the rising threat of tech-heavy Chinese automakers. The promises are big: GM claims it will use AI to cut vehicle development times in half, introduce compute units up to 40 times more powerful than its current hardware, model next-gen battery chemistries in record time, and bring eyes-off autonomous driving to its top-selling trucks and SUVs. In short, GM wants to transition from a legacy automaker into an AI-driven tech enterprise, leveraging its massive scale across both electric and gas-powered fleets. It’s a bold strategy, even if we’ve heard variations of it before. [Image: Faster R&D and digital factory twins For decades, GM has wrestled with sluggish four- to five-year vehicle development cycles that lag behind the light-speed pace of consumer tech. The company tried to bridge that divide with aggressive EV targets and software like Super Cruise. But as software-defined architecture evolved from an industry buzzword into a table-stakes requirement, maintaining fragmented vehicle platforms and dozens of disparate control units began to severely drag down engineering efforts. Now, GM says it’s aiming to slice that development cycle down to just two years using “digital thread virtualization.” Instead of operating in silos or relying on slow, step-by-step handoffs, the company says it will unify design, engineering, and manufacturing digitally from day one. (We’ve already reported on GM’s efforts to inject AI directly into its vehicle design process.) GM points to its new battery development program as proof of concept. The automaker tested over 300,000 virtual battery designs before building a single physical prototype, eventually settling on a lithium manganese rich (LMR) chemistry. That virtual process let GM’s battery team go from initial concept to formal approval in just one month. These new LMR cells will power GM’s fourth-generation EV platform. The company claims the cells offer 33 percent higher energy density than traditional lithium iron phosphate cells at a comparable cost alongside a 20 percent boost in efficiency per kilowatt-hour, yielding longer-range EVs without forcing drivers to haul around a heavier pack. The batteries will be produced by Ultium Cells, GM’s joint venture with LG Energy Solution, at its factory in Spring Hill, Tennessee. Beyond the battery, GM engineered the entire powertrain as a single integrated system. The new drive units feature 40 percent fewer internal parts than current hardware. Because the drivetrain is lighter and takes up significantly less space, future cabins theoretically should offer more room for passengers and cargo. [Image: A single, liquid-cooled brain To fix its messy electronic setup, GM is replacing dozens of small, scattered electronic control units and heavy wiring harnesses with a single central computer. GM claims this unified unit — which is liquid-cooled and connected by high-speed lines — delivers 40 times the computing power while stripping out 30 percent of the physical wiring. That extra horsepower should translate into snappier screens, smarter voice controls, and seamless over-the-air (OTA) updates for automated driving features and battery management. Granted, GM has been promising smarter cars and faster software updates for years. The automaker launched a “digital nerve system” in the 2020 Cadillac CT5 and later rolled out its Ultifi software platform with big promises about OTA capabilities. While drivers generally give GM high marks for hardware dependability, the company’s software rollout has faced its fair share of stumbles and consumer frustration over unnecessary complexity. (Remember the disastrous Chevy Blazer rollout?) GM is extending this digital integration to the factory floor with a project dubbed — and capitalized rather oddly — “PlantBrAIn.” By pairing real-time factory floor data with digital-twin simulations across stamping, casting, welding, painting, and assembly, GM hopes workers can catch physical errors and equipment bottlenecks in a virtual model before they disrupt actual production. [Image: Personal autonomy — and an autonomous dry-cleaning pickup? GM’s newly upgraded compute platform will make its production debut in 2028 on the Cadillac Escalade IQ — the same vehicle GM announced last year would be the first to receive its hands-free, eyes-off highway driving system. (Given that GM teased this centralized compute platform last year, today’s hardware announcement is a bit of a retread.) However, GM isn’t keeping its eyes-off tech locked behind the price tag of a $120,000 luxury SUV. The automaker confirmed plans to roll out hands-free, eyes-off highway driving across its broader lineup, spanning both EVs and gas-powered models. As GM puts it: > Our vision is to build vehicles that can drive themselves or their occupants anywhere they need to be. This includes a future where your vehicle can handle mundane tasks for you, like heading out into bumper-to-bumper traffic to pick up groceries or dry cleaning, giving you valuable time back. An uncrewed pickup truck executing a dry-cleaning run through morning traffic is certainly a vision, though one we’ll need to see to believe. GM also teased a futuristic vision for autonomous cabins called “Concept Horizon,” which reimagines the interior as an open space purely dedicated to relaxing, working, or unwinding. [Image: Overhauling OnStar for its 30th birthday Finally, GM is celebrating OnStar’s 30th anniversary by giving the iconic service a massive AI overhaul. Rather than acting strictly as a backup button for roadside emergencies, OnStar is being rebranded as an active, AI-driven intelligence platform. Drivers can trigger the new OnStar AI Assistant by saying, “Hey OnStar” to tweak cabin temperatures, open the glove box, pop the EV charge port, or check tire pressure and battery diagnostics. The assistant will debut on the 2027 Cadillac Lyriq through an OTA update before expanding to other models. While GM previously rolled out Google’s Gemini-powered voice assistant to 2022 and newer models, this new OnStar assistant operates at a deeper system level. Unlike Gemini, it can execute physical vehicle functions and run hardware-level diagnostics, such as managing specific HVAC zones, interpreting dashboard warning lights, or running battery health checks on the fly. GM’s vision of a central, AI-driven vehicle architecture is undeniably ambitious, and if it works, it could genuinely streamline how cars are built and updated. But for an automaker that has spent years pitching software transformations while occasionally stumbling, execution remains everything. Until an uncrewed Silverado actually pulls into a suburban driveway with a load of fresh dry cleaning, drivers will likely treat these grand AI promises like any other product roadmap: best taken with a healthy dose of patience.

articles.title: Your phone can alert you when prices drop. Here's how
articles.summary: Safari's Notify Me feature and Google's price-tracking tools can monitor products and send alerts when prices drop on your iPhone or Android.
articles.body: Have you ever found something you wanted to buy, only to wonder whether the price might drop next week? Maybe it's a new pair of headphones, a kitchen appliance or a gift you've had your eye on. You could keep checking the website every day, but who has time for that? Here's something you may not realize. Your phone can help watch prices for you. Apple's Safari browser has a feature that monitors website changes, while Google's shopping tools offer price tracking on supported products. That means you can spend less time refreshing product listings and more time deciding whether a deal is actually worth your money. I'll show you how to set up these alerts on an Apple iPhone, Samsung Galaxy and Google Pixel. Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Join us Saturday, October 31, at 11 AM ET / 8 AM PT. Register free now at CyberGuyLive.com. 8 SERIOUSLY ANNOYING TASKS YOU CAN HAND OFF TO AN AI AGENT How to get price-drop alerts on iPhone running iOS 27 Apple introduced a feature called Notify Me in Safari with iOS 27. Instead of returning to a website to see whether something has changed, you can tell Safari what to watch. For example, you might ask Safari to notify you when a pair of headphones drops below $150. You could also monitor a sold-out item and get an alert when the website indicates it's available again. Unlike a traditional price tracker, Safari can look for other changes on a webpage, too. However, the feature doesn't work with every website, and alerts depend on Safari detecting the requested change. Important: Notify Me requires Apple Intelligence. It works on compatible models, including the iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max and iPhone 16 or later. The standard iPhone 15 and iPhone 15 Plus do not support Apple Intelligence. Steps to set up Safari Notify Me Safari checks the page at your selected interval and sends a notification when it detects the change you requested. The available checking intervals include hourly, daily, weekly and monthly options. You can also use Notify Me for something other than shopping, such as watching for event tickets or a registration page to open. Just remember that updates are not necessarily instantaneous. Can you track prices on an iPhone without Apple Intelligence? Yes. If you have a standard iPhone 15 or another model that doesn't support Safari Notify Me, you can use Google Chrome instead. Google offers Chrome price tracking on iPhones running iOS 15 or later, including iOS 27. It works on supported product pages and requires a signed-in Google Account, history synchronization and the necessary browsing settings. Steps to track prices using Chrome on iPhone To manage tracked products, look for Track Price in Chrome's three-dot menu. You may also find alert controls under Chrome > three-dot menu > Settings > Notifications. The exact options can vary by Chrome version and account. Don't see Track Price? The option may not be available for that product or your account. You can also try searching for the product in the Google app and looking for a price-tracking option in its shopping results. ANTI-SCAM SETTINGS ON IPHONE, PIXEL AND GALAXY YOU SHOULD CHECK How to get price-drop alerts on Samsung Galaxy and Google Pixel Samsung Galaxy and Google Pixel owners can use Google's shopping tools to track products and receive alerts when prices fall. The easiest place to start is the Google app, which works similarly on both phones. Chrome may also show price-drop indicators on shopping pages you've left open. How to track a product using the Google app Google can send you a notification on your phone or an email when the product reaches your selected price. Make sure you're signed into your Google Account and have notifications enabled. Don't see Track price? Go back to your search results and tap Shopping near the top of the screen. Select the product you want and look for Track price again. Google doesn't offer price tracking for every product, and the option may not appear for every account. How to track prices directly in Chrome on Android There's another handy option for Samsung Galaxy and Google Pixel owners. Chrome can actively track prices on supported product pages and alert you when they drop. That means you don't have to leave a shopping tab open and keep checking it yourself. Here's how to get started: You can find your tracked items under Chrome > three-dot menu > Bookmarks > Tracked products. To manage alerts, go to Chrome > three-dot menu > Settings > Google services > Get price tracking notifications. From there, you can adjust mobile and email notifications. Keep in mind that this feature only works on supported product pages. You'll also need to be signed into Chrome with your Google Account, enable syncing for tabs and browsing history and turn on Make searches and browsing better. AI SHOPPING CARTS COULD DRIVE UP YOUR GROCERY BILL Google's new Universal Cart adds another way to track prices Google introduced Universal Cart in the United States earlier this month. The feature is rolling out across Google Search and the Gemini app, giving shoppers another way to keep track of products without constantly checking different websites. Universal Cart lets you save items from multiple retailers in one place. Once you've added a product, Google's shopping tools can monitor its price and alert you when the cost drops or an out-of-stock item becomes available again. The cart can also identify promotional codes and suggest payment options that may help you save money. For example, if you're shopping for a new TV, you can save models from different stores and let Google watch for price changes. When you're ready to buy, you can complete eligible purchases through Google Pay or finish checkout directly on the retailer's website. Universal Cart is rolling out in the U.S., so it may not appear in every account immediately. It's another option worth checking if you already use Google Search or Gemini to shop. Why your phone might not show the price-tracking option If you don't see Notify Me or Track price, the feature may be unavailable for your phone, account or shopping website. Start by checking that your apps and browser are updated. On iPhone, Safari Notify Me requires a compatible device with Apple Intelligence enabled. For Google's shopping tools, make sure you're signed into your Google Account. Chrome may also require additional browsing or synchronization settings for certain shopping features. Some product pages simply don't support tracking. In that case, try another retailer's listing for the same item. Google's price-tracking features are available in supported countries, including the United States, although availability varies by product and account. Three things to check before buying after a price alert A lower price can be tempting, especially when a notification pops up while you're doing something else. However, I wouldn't rush to checkout without checking a few details. A price alert tells you something has changed. It doesn't necessarily mean you've found the lowest available price. A quick privacy consideration Price tracking comes with a privacy trade-off worth understanding. Google's shopping tools use your Google Account to manage tracked products and alerts. Certain Chrome shopping features may also require additional browsing information or settings, including Make searches and browsing better. You should review those options before enabling them. That setting allows Chrome to share browsing-related information with Google to improve its services. You can review these options under Chrome > 3 dots in the upper right >Settings > Google services. Apple's Safari Notify Me uses Apple Intelligence to monitor webpages for requested changes. Before enabling either feature, consider whether the convenience is worth the information and permissions involved. One more shopping safety tip Be careful about clicking price-drop alerts or shopping links from unfamiliar senders. Scammers can create fake sale notifications that lead to fraudulent websites. Strong antivirus software can provide an additional layer of protection by helping detect malicious links, phishing attempts and other online threats. Kurt's key takeaways I've lost count of how many times I've looked at something online, decided to wait and then completely forgotten to check whether the price dropped. That's why I like having my phone do some of the watching for me. With Safari's Notify Me feature in iOS 27, compatible iPhones can monitor more than just prices. Meanwhile, Google's shopping tools can help Samsung Galaxy and Pixel owners follow prices on supported products, while Chrome offers additional shopping features on compatible devices. My advice is to start with something you actually need, especially a larger purchase where a price drop could save you a meaningful amount. Set up an alert and see what happens. You might save some money without spending your evenings hunting through shopping websites. Have you ever bought something only to see the price drop a few days later?
